passage: I'm Farida, and I noticed it first in my head: whenever Nandini spoke in meetings I heard a sneer. "Here she goes again." I rolled my eyes inwardly, and once, a little, outwardly. I didn't like who that made me. So I named it to myself, contempt, and took a break before the next meeting by walking around the block. Then I asked Nandini for coffee and said, "When you send the long updates, I find myself getting impatient. Can we agree on a short summary first?" She looked startled, then said, "I didn't realise. Sure, a summary first works." The sneer didn't vanish, but it lost some of its grip. I've stopped rehearsing her flaws in my head.

qa.q: Where did Farida walk before the next meeting?
qa.a: Around the block.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on hearing the sneer inside?
qa.a: Contempt and impatience towards Nandini, and discomfort at feeling it.

qa.q: What made Farida's coffee conversation constructive?
qa.a: Farida described Farida's own reaction to the behaviour without insults and proposed a concrete fix.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt when Farida raised the topic?
qa.a: Startled at first, but her "I didn't realise" suggests she was open to it.

grounding: A young adult notices contempt in their own thoughts about a colleague, names it, takes a break and raises the concern respectfully.

passage: Note from Preeti, senior manager. Vijay asked for ten minutes after the sprint review. He said he had been catching himself rolling his eyes at a teammate's sloppy commits, and that a thought like "he doesn't even care" kept repeating. He had taken a walk each afternoon and written down what specifically bothered him: missing tests, no notes. Then he had asked the teammate to pair on the next task and add a short checklist. I told Vijay to keep raising the concern respectfully and privately, and to tell me if it does not ease, because contempt can wear a team down. I have asked for a review of the checklist in two weeks.

passage:
Thursday
Caught myself doing it again today. Sarika walked in twenty minutes late to the handover, laughing on her phone, and I rolled my eyes so hard my head moved. In my head I called her something I wouldn't say to my worst enemy. That's the third time this week I've felt that sneer rising, a kind of disgust, like she isn't worth taking seriously.
I don't like who I am when I think like that. Rashid Chacha used to say contempt is the fastest way to ruin any team.
So I named it, right there: that's contempt. Then I went out to the car park and walked two rounds before I trusted my face.
After lunch I asked her for five minutes. "When you're late to handover, I miss the updates on the night cases, and it makes my shift harder. Could we agree on 8:45?" She looked surprised, then apologetic. Her bus route had changed. She'll message me if she's running late.
Imran

qa.a: Imran noticed a rising sneer of contempt and disgust, as if she weren't worth taking seriously, and felt uncomfortable about it.

qa.q: How did Imran handle the contempt?
qa.a: Imran named the feeling, took a walk to settle, then raised the specific concern about handover timing respectfully and asked for an agreement.

qa.q: What was going on for Sarika?
qa.a: Her bus route had changed, making her late; she was surprised and apologetic when Imran raised it.

passage: At the dairy cooperative meeting in Anand district, Kavitha-tai interrupted Imran for the third time. "Our city boy with his degree will now teach us how cows work." A few members laughed. Imran felt it rise in him: not just anger but a cold, curling disgust. Stubborn old woman, his mind said, and worse. He heard the words and was shocked at himself. His own grandmother had never been to school either. He said, "Let's take ten minutes for tea," and walked out to the water tank, breathing slowly until the sneer left his face. When they came back, he asked Kavitha-tai to sit with him for a moment, away from the others. "Tai, you know more about these animals than I ever will. When you call me 'city boy' in front of everyone, members stop listening to the plan. I'd rather we argue about the fodder plan, not about me." She eyed him for a long moment. "Fine. Your fodder plan is wrong. Let me tell you why." And she did, sharply and usefully.

qa.q: How many times had Kavitha-tai interrupted Imran?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What did Imran feel when Kavitha-tai mocked him?
qa.a: Imran noticed anger and a cold, curling disgust and contempt, and was shocked at the dismissive words in his head.

qa.q: How did Imran regulate the contempt and raise the concern?
qa.a: He called a tea break, breathed until the sneer left, then privately acknowledged her knowledge and asked her to argue about the plan, not about him.

qa.q: How did Kavitha-tai respond?
qa.a: She eyed him, agreed, and gave sharp but useful criticism of the fodder plan instead of mocking him.

grounding: Shows a young professional catching contempt in his own thoughts, taking a break, and raising his concern respectfully.

subtype: Contemptuous and disgusted in relationships and work [Regulating]
passage: At the Johannesburg studio where Hana designs packaging, the third late file from Thabo landed at 5:40 on a Friday. She felt her lip curl before she had read a line. Typical. Can't he manage one deadline? Her fingers were already typing a reply with "AGAIN??" in the subject line. She stopped, deleted it, and said under her breath, "That's contempt talking." She took her coffee up to the rooftop, watched the minibus taxis crawl along the street below and let her jaw unclench. On Monday she asked Thabo for ten minutes. "The last three files came in after five, and it's meant weekend work for me. Can we look at what's getting in the way?" Thabo rubbed the back of his neck. "The client sends changes at four. I've been too embarrassed to push back." They drafted a two o'clock cut-off together, and Hana found she could look him in the eye again.

qa.q: What time did Thabo's third late file land?
qa.a: It landed at 5:40 on a Friday.

qa.q: What does Hana's curled lip and the "AGAIN??" subject line suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely contempt and frustration at Thabo after more weekend work, though end-of-week tiredness could also have sharpened her reaction.

qa.q: What small step helped Hana before she replied?
qa.a: She named the feeling as contempt, deleted the harsh draft and took a break on the rooftop, so on Monday she could raise the late files calmly.

qa.q: How might Thabo have felt if the "AGAIN??" email had gone out on Friday?
qa.a: He would likely have felt attacked and even more embarrassed, and might have kept hiding the four o'clock client changes instead of admitting them.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult catching contempt toward a colleague, pausing, and then raising the concern with respect.
